lessons.name: API Keys & .env
lessons.desc: Get a key, keep it secret, load it safely — never commit it
lessons.what:
An API key is your credential for the LLM provider — it is tied to your account and your wallet. You store it in a .env file (never in source code) and load it at runtime with a library like dotenv.

🧠 Analogy: the key to your apartment. The .env file is the locked drawer in the closet — the code never knows the key directly, it asks the drawer.
lessons.why:
Every later project in this journal needs this exact setup. Getting it right once — and keeping the key off GitHub — saves you money, embarrassment, and a banned account.

Kaise karna hai:

You will do this in the very first problem below: create .env, add .env to .gitignore, and load it with dotenv.
gotchas: Committing a key to git is the classic beginner mistake — put .env in .gitignore before you even create the file.
Keys are per-provider (OpenAI vs Anthropic) — do not mix them up.
If a key leaks publicly, revoke it immediately in the dashboard and roll a new one.

lessons.name: Your First SDK Call
lessons.desc: Install the SDK, make a chat request, read the response
lessons.what:
An SDK (e.g. openai or @anthropic-ai/sdk) wraps the raw HTTP API in nice functions. A minimal chat call: create a client, send a messages array, get back the assistant's reply and token usage.

🧠 Analogy: the SDK is a well-labeled dashboard instead of a box of loose wires — same machine, far fewer ways to electrocute yourself.
lessons.why:
Before building an agent, you must be comfortable with the one primitive everything is built on: one request in, one reply out.

Kaise karna hai:

The First LLM Call problem walks you through install → client → request → print → explain the response fields.
gotchas: Install the SDK in the right directory and check Node version — some SDKs need Node 18+.
The reply lives at message.content — printing the whole object confuses beginners.
Pass model exactly as named on the provider — a typo means a 404-style error.

lessons.name: Errors, Rate Limits & Retries
lessons.desc: 429s, timeouts, and the retry-with-backoff habit
lessons.what:
LLM APIs fail all the time: rate limits (429), timeouts, and transient 5xx errors. The fix is a retry with exponential backoff — wait a little, try again, wait more, cap the attempts.

🧠 Analogy: busy phone line — you do not hang up and cry, you wait a moment and redial, each time a bit longer between attempts.
lessons.why:
Every agent you build will hit rate limits. Knowing the retry pattern now means your later agents survive real load instead of crashing.

Kaise karna hai:

The First LLM Call problem has you catch errors, sleep, and retry — the same pattern returns in Mini-opencode Phase 1 error handling.
gotchas: Do NOT retry instantly and in a tight loop — that makes rate limits worse. Back off.
Read the error message before retrying: a 401 (bad key) will never succeed on retry.
Cap attempts (e.g. 3) and log the final failure — infinite retries burn money.

lessons.name: LLMs & Tokens
lessons.desc: How language models work — tokens, context window, temperature, top-p, stop sequences
lessons.what:
A language model predicts the next token. It reads your prompt as a sequence of tokens (word pieces) and, at each step, picks the most likely continuation. temperature controls randomness, top-p trims unlikely options, and the context window is how much text it can "see" at once.

🧠 Analogy: an extremely well-read autocomplete. It does not "know" facts — it knows what text usually follows other text.
lessons.why:
Every agent budget is measured in tokens, and the context window is the single biggest constraint on how much of your repo the agent can hold at once.

Kaise karna hai:

You will watch token counts in Mini-opencode Phase 1: tokens_in + tokens_out per call, and trimming history as it nears the window.
gotchas: Higher temperature = more creative but less reliable — use 0 for tool calls, higher only for chat.
Tokens are not words — a long identifier can be many tokens; never estimate by character count.
The context window counts input AND output — a huge reply can silently hit the limit.

lessons.name: Prompt Engineering
lessons.desc: System prompts, user prompts, few-shot examples, role assignment, output constraints
lessons.what:
Prompt engineering is writing the instructions that steer the model. System prompts set the rules ("You are a code reviewer..."), user prompts give the task, few-shot examples show the desired format, and negative constraints say what not to do.

🧠 Analogy: the system prompt is an employee handbook; the user prompt is today's assignment. The handbook decides how the assignment gets done.
lessons.why:
In a coding agent, the system prompt is where behavior lives — what tools exist, how to format output, when to stop. It is the highest-leverage text you will write.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode composes its system prompt from parts: base rules + tool list + loaded skills (Phase 6). You will build and swap them as context demands.
gotchas: Vague instructions get vague behavior — be explicit about format and stopping conditions.
Negative instructions ("do not use bullet points") are often ignored — reframe positively.
Long system prompts burn context — keep rules tight and move details into skills.

lessons.name: API Basics
lessons.desc: OpenAI / Anthropic SDK — auth, request structure, roles array, response parsing, rate limits
lessons.what:
The API is how you talk to the model. You send a request with a model name and a messages array (roles system, user, assistant) plus parameters like temperature. The SDK returns the reply, token usage, and more.

🧠 Analogy: a phone line to the intern. What you say is the request; what they say back is the response. You must write down the whole conversation (messages) every time — the intern has no memory.
lessons.why:
Every agent is just a loop of API calls. Knowing the request/response shape — and how to read errors and rate limits — is the prerequisite for everything else.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode wraps the OpenAI/Anthropic SDK in one thin LLM class so you can swap models without touching the loop (capstone Phase 1).
gotchas: Always send the full message history, not just the new question — the API is stateless.
The system message must come first in the array.
Rate limits (429) are normal — retry with backoff instead of crashing.

lessons.name: Streaming Responses
lessons.desc: ReadableStream, Server-Sent Events, incremental token rendering in the UI
lessons.what:
Streaming sends tokens to you as the model generates them instead of waiting for the full reply. In Node you async-iterate over chunks; in the browser you read response.body and append each delta.

🧠 Analogy: batch is a letter delivered when finished; streaming is a phone call where the person talks word by word.
lessons.why:
For a CLI agent, streaming is what makes it feel alive — you see reasoning in real time instead of staring at a spinner.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 1 (The Shell) prints a token stream to the terminal and lets you interrupt it with Ctrl+C — the base of a real agent UX.
gotchas: Accumulate the full text as you go — the stream only gives deltas, not the final message.
Handle aborted streams — a cancelled request may leave a half-written message.
Append to the buffer instead of re-rendering the whole thing each chunk.

lessons.name: Structured Output
lessons.desc: JSON mode, function calling for extraction, Zod schema validation, retry on parse fail
lessons.what:
Structured output forces the model to return JSON (or a schema-valid object) instead of free text. You use a JSON-mode flag, a function-calling schema, or prefill the reply — then validate with a parser like Zod.

🧠 Analogy: you asked the intern for a report; structured output is the fill-in-the-blanks form you hand them so their answer is usable without you re-parsing prose.
lessons.why:
Agents cannot reliably parse prose. Every tool call and every subagent handoff in Mini-opencode is a structured message — malformed output breaks the chain.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 1 validates model JSON with Zod and retries up to 3 times, feeding the parse error back so the model fixes itself.
gotchas: The model can still emit invalid JSON — never skip validation.
Describe the exact shape in the prompt too; JSON mode alone does not guarantee the shape.
On failure, pass the error back into the prompt rather than silently re-sending the same request.

lessons.name: ReAct Pattern
lessons.desc: Reason → Act → Observe — the fundamental loop that turns completions into agents
lessons.what:
ReAct (Reason + Act) is the pattern where the model explicitly thinks (Thought:), picks an action (Action: search(...)), observes the result, and repeats until it produces a final answer.

🧠 Analogy: solving a mystery — think, check a clue, update your theory, check the next clue.
lessons.why:
This is the seed of the agentic loop. ReAct gives the model a scratchpad so its reasoning, actions, and observations stay coherent across many steps.

Kaise karna hai:

You build the raw version in AI journal Phase 2, then refine it into the while-loop that powers Mini-opencode's hands (capstone Phase 2).
gotchas: The Observation is injected by your code after running the tool — never let the model fabricate it.
Without a max-steps guard, ReAct agents can loop forever.
The scratchpad counts against the context window — long chains need trimming.

lessons.name: Tool / Function Definition
lessons.desc: JSON schema for tools — name, description, parameters. Description quality is everything.
lessons.what:
A tool is a function you expose to the model via a JSON schema: name, description, and parameters. The model reads the description to decide when to call it; your code implements the actual work.

🧠 Analogy: you hand the intern a phone book with descriptions — "call this number for accounting, this one for IT." The intern never dials; you dial.
lessons.why:
The description is the model's entire understanding of the tool. A bad one means the right tool is never chosen. Tool design is 80% of agent quality.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 2 defines tools like read_file, edit_file, and bash with rich descriptions, called from inside the loop.
gotchas: A vague description ("search") gets misused; a specific one ("search for text using ripgrep...") gets used correctly.
The schema must match your parser exactly — wrong types break the tool call.
Too many overlapping tools confuse the model — keep the set small and distinct.

lessons.name: The Agentic Loop
lessons.desc: while-not-done loop: call LLM → check for tool call → execute → append result → repeat
lessons.what:
The agentic loop: call the LLM → if it requests a tool, run it and append the result → repeat → until it answers without a tool call. This is the heart of every coding agent.

🧠 Analogy: you sit beside a brilliant intern who cannot touch the computer. They ask for a fact, you fetch it, read it aloud, they decide what to look up next.
lessons.why:
Frameworks (LangChain, Vercel AI SDK) are just this loop in a box. Building it once yourself means you can debug and extend anything.

Kaise karna hai:

You write this loop from scratch in AI journal Phase 1/2; Mini-opencode Phase 2 makes it production-grade with guards, logging, and iteration limits.
gotchas: The tool result MUST go back into messages or the model forgets what it just did.
Always set max_iterations — a confused model can loop forever.
Return errors as tool output, not thrown exceptions, so the model can recover.

lessons.name: Memory Types
lessons.desc: In-context, episodic (external DB), semantic (vector store), procedural (system prompt)
lessons.what:
Agents remember four ways: in-context (current messages), episodic (conversations in an external DB), semantic (facts in a vector store), and procedural (behavior in the system prompt).

🧠 Analogy: in-context is working memory, episodic is a diary, semantic is a library, procedural is habits.
lessons.why:
A good agent picks the right memory for the job — cheap and immediate for in-context, durable and searchable for semantic.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode uses in-context as the main store, trims it when full, and later loads skills (procedural) — while your AI journal Phase 1 problem exercises episodic memory in a real DB.
gotchas: Confusing semantic memory (facts) with episodic memory (events) leads to wrong retrieval.
Stored memory is useless without structure — you need a way to find it again.
In-context is not durable — refresh it from storage when a session resumes.

lessons.name: Conversation History Management
lessons.desc: Token limits, history summarization, sliding window, message trimming strategies
lessons.what:
LLMs have a fixed context window, so history must be managed: count tokens, trim old messages, summarize the middle, and keep the most recent turns verbatim.

🧠 Analogy: a small whiteboard. You erase old scribbles and write a one-line summary so the important stuff still fits.
lessons.why:
Unmanaged history either blows the context window (API error) or floods it with noise (worse answers).

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode tracks tokens per call and compresses when full — the same strategy your "Conversation Memory Bot" problem builds in AI journal Phase 1.
gotchas: Never drop the system prompt or the latest user question.
Summaries lose detail — keep recent turns verbatim and summarize only the old middle.
Token counting needs a real tokenizer or honest estimate; character counts lie.

lessons.name: Embeddings
lessons.desc: Text → dense vector. What they represent, how to generate them, cosine similarity
lessons.what:
An embedding turns text into a list of numbers (a vector) that captures meaning — similar texts get similar vectors. You compare them with cosine similarity to find related content.

🧠 Analogy: every sentence maps to a point in space; sentences with similar meaning land near each other.
lessons.why:
Embeddings let you search "by meaning" instead of exact words — the basis of semantic search and vector RAG.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 4 explains why code retrieval mostly uses grep instead (exact symbols beat fuzzy similarity), while embeddings still power the doc-Q&A path in your AI journal Phase 1 problem.
gotchas: Cosine similarity needs normalized vectors; raw dot products are not comparable.
Do not mix vectors from different embedding models in one index.
An embedding captures meaning, not facts — it finds related text, it does not reason about it.

lessons.name: Vector Databases
lessons.desc: Pinecone, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate — indexing, ANN search, metadata filtering
lessons.what:
A vector database stores embeddings and finds nearest neighbors fast using ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) indexes like HNSW or IVF, plus metadata filters.

🧠 Analogy: a library card catalog organized by meaning — you describe the book and it points you to the right shelf.
lessons.why:
Vector DBs make semantic search scale to millions of chunks with sub-100ms lookups — the engine behind RAG.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 1/3 problems use pgvector or Qdrant for document Q&A; Mini-opencode Phase 4 deliberately skips vectors for code — grep wins — which is a key insight of the capstone.
gotchas: ANN is approximate — tune recall vs speed for your data.
Metadata filters (file, date, source) are essential; raw similarity alone is noisy.
For tiny datasets a plain array scan is faster — add a DB only when you need scale.

lessons.name: Agentic Loop from Scratch
lessons.desc: Implement the full while-loop without frameworks. Understand every line before using abstractions.
lessons.what:
Writing the while-loop yourself with raw SDK calls — no framework. You parse tool calls, run them, append results, and loop until the model answers.

🧠 Analogy: you build the machine that moves the intern's hands. The model reasons; your loop is the only thing that can act.
lessons.why:
Frameworks hide this. When something misbehaves in production, you must know exactly what the loop does — that is the difference between a user and a builder.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 2 is precisely this: a hand-rolled loop with iteration guards, per-step logging, and clean stop conditions.
gotchas: Handle both API flavors: OpenAI finish_reason === "tool_calls" vs Anthropic stop_reason === "tool_use".
An LLM can request several tools in one response — be ready for arrays.
Log every step; an invisible loop is undebuggable.

lessons.name: ReAct Implementation
lessons.desc: Thought → Action → Observation format. How to structure prompts so the model reasons before acting.
lessons.what:
ReAct with an explicit scratchpad: the model writes Thought/Action/Observation lines, your code parses the action (regex), injects the real observation, and loops until "Final Answer".

🧠 Analogy: a detective's notebook — every hypothesis and every clue check is written down so the chain of reasoning stays visible.
lessons.why:
The explicit scratchpad keeps the model honest and your steps auditable — you can see exactly why it chose each action.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 2 problem "ReAct Agent from Scratch" builds the parser; Mini-opencode Phase 2/5 refines it into plan mode and structured tool calls.
gotchas: Parse the action line, not the thought — the model sometimes narrates without acting.
Inject observations yourself; never trust the model to "remember" the tool result.
Guard with a max step count so a confused agent cannot run forever.

lessons.name: Planning Strategies
lessons.desc: Task decomposition, step-by-step planning, plan validation, re-planning on failure
lessons.what:
Planning means the agent decomposes a task into steps before acting: write a plan, execute step by step, validate, and re-plan when a step fails.

🧠 Analogy: a blueprint before hammering. A good plan catches missing details early and avoids wasted tool calls.
lessons.why:
Complex tasks ("add auth to this app") fail when the agent improvises; planning cuts errors and makes progress visible.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 5 (The Planner) adds a dedicated plan mode that writes a JSON step list — and only then lets the agent act — mirroring opencode's plan/act modes.
gotchas: Plans go stale — re-plan when a step fails instead of pushing through.
Keep plans small and concrete; a giant plan burns the whole context window.
Validate the plan format (JSON schema) before executing it.

lessons.name: Error Recovery & Retries
lessons.desc: Tool failures, invalid JSON, API timeouts — teach the agent to diagnose and retry
lessons.what:
Teaching the agent to handle failures: tool timeouts, invalid JSON, API errors. Instead of crashing, the agent reads the error, diagnoses, and retries with a fix.

🧠 Analogy: the intern calls you with "that lookup failed" — you read them the error text and let them decide what to try next.
lessons.why:
Real agents fail constantly. Recovery is the difference between a demo and something that finishes the task overnight.

Kaise karna hai:

Feed errors back as observations and let the model propose a fix — with bounded retries. Mini-opencode gates retries and knows when to stop and ask for help.
gotchas: Always bound retries (e.g. 3 attempts) — infinite self-correction is expensive.
Include the actual error text in the prompt; a vague "it failed" does not help.
After repeated failure, stop and surface the error to the human instead of thrashing.

lessons.name: Human-in-the-Loop
lessons.desc: Pause points, approval gates, interrupt handling — how to add a human review step
lessons.what:
Pausing the agent before risky actions (editing files, running commands, sending emails) so a human approves, edits, or rejects first. Some tools are auto-approved; dangerous ones always gate.

🧠 Analogy: the intern drafts the email, but you press send. You trust them to write; you keep control of what ships.
lessons.why:
Safety. The worst agent failure is not a wrong answer — it is rm -rf src because a prompt told it to. Gates make a harness safe to run on your real repo.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 2 adds approval for edits and Phase 3 sandboxes bash; a blocklist (rm -rf, sudo, git push) overrides even approved actions.
gotchas: Gates must be enforced by the harness, not requested by the model.
Give the human enough context to decide: what, where, and why.
An allowlist of safe tools keeps the UX from becoming a click-farm.

lessons.name: Parallel Tool Calls
lessons.desc: Running multiple tools concurrently, Promise.all patterns, merging parallel results
lessons.what:
Running several independent tool calls at once (Promise.all / allSettled) instead of one at a time, then merging the results.

🧠 Analogy: not making 5 phone calls back-to-back — you hire 5 people to call in parallel and collect all answers.
lessons.why:
Latency. If the agent needs weather + news + calendar, sequential calls take 3× as long; parallel makes it feel instant.

Kaise karna hai:

Many models emit multiple tool calls in one response — your loop should execute them concurrently. Your AI journal Phase 2 "Parallel Research Agent" problem measures the speedup.
gotchas: Use allSettled (not all) so one failing call does not kill the rest.
Only parallelize independent calls — results that feed each other must stay sequential.
Cap concurrency to respect rate limits; 5 parallel calls can 429 you.

lessons.name: Chunking Strategies
lessons.desc: Fixed-size, recursive character, semantic chunking, overlap, parent-child chunks
lessons.what:
Splitting documents into retrievable pieces: fixed-size with overlap, recursive character splitting, semantic (by meaning boundaries), and parent-child (small chunks retrieved, larger parent given as context).

🧠 Analogy: cutting a book into cards. Too big and a card is off-topic; too small and a card loses its meaning.
lessons.why:
Chunk size is the biggest retrieval quality lever — too big dilutes relevance, too small loses context.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 3 problems exercise each strategy; the insight for Mini-opencode is that code chunks by function/class (AST), not by token count.
gotchas: Overlap prevents cutting a sentence (or function) in half.
Chunk boundaries that ignore structure (sentences, code) hurt retrieval badly.
Store metadata (source, page, index) with every chunk or you cannot cite or filter.

lessons.name: Embedding Models
lessons.desc: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small/large, Cohere, Sentence Transformers, dimensionality tradeoffs
lessons.what:
Models that convert text to vectors — OpenAI text-embedding-3-small/large, Cohere, Sentence Transformers. Tradeoffs: cost, dimensionality, multilingual support, accuracy.

🧠 Analogy: different mapmakers. A cheap map might skip alleys; an expensive one captures every street.
lessons.why:
Your retrieval quality caps at your embedding quality — a cheap model can silently lose meaning.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 1/3 problems pick a model and measure; you will learn to batch-embed (~100 at a time) to dodge rate limits.
gotchas: Never mix vectors from different embedding models in one index.
Higher dimensions cost more and are not always more accurate — test, do not assume.
Embed in the same style you query — chunk-style text in, chunk-style query out.

lessons.name: Similarity Search & ANN
lessons.desc: Cosine similarity, dot product, HNSW, IVF — how vector DBs find nearest neighbors fast
lessons.what:
Finding nearest neighbors by vector distance — cosine similarity for search, and ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) that trade a little accuracy for huge speedups at scale.

🧠 Analogy: finding the closest gas stations. In a small town you check all of them; in a city you use a map index that narrows the search.
lessons.why:
Linear scans die at scale; ANN is how real products search millions of chunks in milliseconds.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 3 problems hit this as the doc set grows — you pick an index type and measure recall vs speed.
gotchas: ANN is approximate — tune index params (ef, M, nlist) against your recall target.
Normalize vectors if you use cosine; some databases expect it.
Pure similarity returns duplicates and off-topic hits — always add metadata filters.

lessons.name: Hybrid Search
lessons.desc: BM25 keyword + vector dense retrieval combined via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)
lessons.what:
Combining keyword search (BM25 — great for exact names and acronyms) with dense vector search (great for meaning), merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

🧠 Analogy: asking both a librarian who knows exact titles AND one who understands topics — then combining their shortlists.
lessons.why:
Pure vector search misses exact matches; pure keyword misses paraphrases. Hybrid gets both, and RRF merges ranks without score normalization.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 3 "Hybrid Search RAG" problem builds it and benchmarks against vector-only to see the lift.
gotchas: RRF formula: score = Σ 1/(k + rank), with k = 60 — no normalization needed.
Run both retrievers concurrently; do not duplicate work.
Hybrid helps most on jargon-heavy corpora (code, medicine, law) — test it on yours.

lessons.name: Reranking
lessons.desc: Cross-encoder reranking (Cohere Rerank, FlashRank) — second-pass scoring for precision
lessons.what:
A second-pass cross-encoder that scores query+document pairs together to reorder the top candidates — far more accurate than the bi-encoder first pass.

🧠 Analogy: a first-pass recruiter shortlists 20 resumes; a senior engineer then reads each against the job description to pick the best 5.
lessons.why:
Retrieval is recall; reranking is precision. Retrieve top-20, rerank to top-5, and only the best context reaches the LLM.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 3 "Multi-source Research" problem shows rerankers promoting results from position 15+ into the top 5.
gotchas: A reranker ranks a candidate list — it does not retrieve.
Cross-encoders are slow — rerank ~20–100 candidates, never your whole corpus.
If the first pass misses a relevant document entirely, no reranker can save it.

lessons.name: RAG Evaluation
lessons.desc: Context recall, answer faithfulness, answer relevancy — RAGAS framework metrics
lessons.what:
Measuring RAG quality: context recall (did we retrieve the right chunks?), answer faithfulness (is the answer grounded in the context?), and answer relevancy — via RAGAS or LLM-as-judge.

🧠 Analogy: a chef tasting every dish before it leaves the kitchen — you cannot improve what you do not measure.
lessons.why:
Evals catch regressions when you change chunking, prompts, or models — and they tell you WHICH part of the pipeline is failing.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 3 problem builds a 30-question golden set and finds its top 3 failure modes; the same discipline powers Mini-opencode Phase 8 evals.
gotchas: Faithfulness fails when the model hallucinates beyond context — the #1 RAG failure.
LLM-as-judge needs calibration — compare against human scores on a sample first.
A small hand-built dataset beats no dataset; grow it as you find failures.

lessons.name: Vercel AI SDK
lessons.desc: useChat, useCompletion, streamText, generateObject, tool rendering in React
lessons.what:
A framework for AI apps in Next.js: streamText on the server, useChat on the client, generateObject for structured output, and built-in tool rendering in React.

🧠 Analogy: a pre-built cockpit — the same dials you would hand-wire, but assembled and tested for you.
lessons.why:
It removes boilerplate (streaming, message state, tool invocations) so you can ship an agent UI in hours — worth knowing even though Mini-opencode is raw.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 4 problem builds a full chat app; the mental model (server stream, client tool rendering) maps directly onto your own CLI loop.
gotchas: maxSteps is what enables multi-step tool behavior — without it the loop stops after one tool call.
Tool results render via toolInvocations, not by re-running the tool client-side.
Understand the stream it hides — you must know how to fall back to raw reads when debugging.

lessons.name: LangGraph Basics
lessons.desc: Nodes, edges, conditional routing, state annotations, compile() and invoke()
lessons.what:
A graph runtime for agents: nodes are functions, edges define flow, state is a shared object, and you compile() then invoke(). Conditional edges route based on state.

🧠 Analogy: a flowchart that runs — every box is a function, every arrow is a decision.
lessons.why:
It makes agent control flow explicit and inspectable — loops and branches become visible instead of buried in while loops.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 4 problem models a research pipeline as a graph; you will see how conditional routing maps onto the if/else logic in your own loop.
gotchas: Nodes receive full state and return updates — mutate nothing, return everything.
Graphs are for control flow, not for hiding complexity — keep nodes small.
Invoke with a config to resume/checkpoint; plain calls lose state.

lessons.name: LangGraph State Machines
lessons.desc: Cyclic graphs, loops, human interrupt nodes, checkpointing with MemorySaver
lessons.what:
Cyclic graphs with loops, conditional edges, human interrupt nodes, and checkpointing (MemorySaver/SqliteSaver) that persist state between runs and resumes.

🧠 Analogy: a recipe you can pause mid-step, put in the fridge, and continue the next day without losing progress.
lessons.why:
Real agents loop and pause. State machines make "retry on low quality" or "ask a human" first-class, not a hack.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 4 problem uses interrupt() for a human gate and conditional quality edges — the same ideas Mini-opencode implements by hand.
gotchas: interrupt() returns control to the caller; resume with the right config or state is lost.
Checkpointing persists state — skipping it silently breaks long-running agents.
Loop edges need explicit exit conditions or the graph never terminates.

lessons.name: Orchestrator + Subagent Pattern
lessons.desc: Master agent delegates tasks to specialist subagents, aggregates results
lessons.what:
A master agent decides which specialist subagents to call (each with focused tools/prompts), then aggregates their structured results into a final answer.

🧠 Analogy: a team lead who never codes — they assign tickets to specialists and merge the pull requests.
lessons.why:
Focus beats breadth. A narrow subagent with one job outperforms a generalist doing five — and you can run them in parallel.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 4 problem builds CodeAgent/DocsAgent/TestAgent under an orchestrator; Mini-opencode Phase 7 (The Team) reuses the exact pattern.
gotchas: Subagents must return structured output your orchestrator can parse.
Keep subagent system prompts narrow — more focus, better results.
Handle one subagent failing without failing the whole orchestration.

lessons.name: CrewAI & Role-based Agents
lessons.desc: Crews, agents with roles/goals/backstory, tasks with context, delegation
lessons.what:
A framework where agents are roles with role, goal, and backstory, organized into Crews with tasks that can delegate (e.g. an Editor sending work back to a Writer).

🧠 Analogy: a theatre troupe — each actor knows their character and objective, and the play emerges from their interactions.
lessons.why:
It is a fast way to prototype multi-agent teams and shows how role personality shapes behavior — useful patterns even if you roll your own.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 4 problem runs a Researcher→Writer→Editor crew; you will steal the delegation idea for your subagent team.
gotchas: Backstories shape behavior more than you expect — keep them purposeful.
Delegation without bounds can loop — cap revisions.
Role-based agents are ergonomic, not magic — the loop underneath is still the same.

lessons.name: Agent Communication & Handoffs
lessons.desc: Shared state, message passing, tool handoffs, result aggregation patterns
lessons.what:
How agents share information: a shared state object, message passing between agents, tool-based handoffs (one agent calls another as a tool), and aggregation of results.

🧠 Analogy: a relay race — the baton (context) must be handed over cleanly or the next runner starts lost.
lessons.why:
The interface between agents IS the design. Clean schemas make teams compose; free-form strings make them break silently.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 7 defines the handoff contract (task + context in, structured result out) — and your AI journal Phase 4 orchestrator problem exercises it.
gotchas: Define a schema for every handoff — free-form text is a debugging nightmare.
Propagate context (goals, constraints) through the chain; each agent resets otherwise.
Shared state that grows unbounded drains the token budget — prune it.

lessons.name: Eval Framework Design
lessons.desc: Defining metrics, building golden datasets, offline vs online evals, regression testing
lessons.what:
A system for measuring your agent: a golden dataset of inputs with expected behavior, metrics (completion rate, quality, efficiency), and offline/online runs — ideally in CI.

🧠 Analogy: a flight simulator before the real flight — you practice against known scenarios and score each landing.
lessons.why:
Agents are stochastic. One good run proves nothing; evals catch regressions when you tweak a prompt or swap a model.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 5 problem builds a nightly eval suite; Mini-opencode Phase 8 (The Verifier) applies the same loop to its own builds.
gotchas: Golden datasets rot — add every failure you find back to the set.
Define metrics before the run; "seems fine" is not a metric.
Run evals in CI so a prompt change cannot silently ship a regression.

lessons.name: LLM-as-Judge
lessons.desc: Using an LLM to score another LLM's output — calibration, criteria, agreement rates
lessons.what:
Using one LLM to score another's output with a rubric (e.g. 1–5 on accuracy, completeness, groundedness) instead of a human.

🧠 Analogy: a trained reviewer who grades essays from the same rubric every time — consistent and fast, but only as good as the rubric.
lessons.why:
It automates quality scoring at scale — the engine behind most modern evals.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 5 evals and Mini-opencode Phase 8 both use a judge prompt that returns {score, reasoning} JSON per sample.
gotchas: Calibrate the judge against human scores (aim for ~80% agreement) or it can drift.
Judges have biases — position, length, sycophancy. Vary order and keep prompts neutral.
Ask for reasoning, not just a number — it is the only way to debug the score.

lessons.name: Observability & Tracing
lessons.desc: LangSmith, Langfuse — span tracking, token/cost logging, trace visualization, alerting
lessons.what:
Recording every LLM call, tool call, and step as spans in a trace (Langfuse, LangSmith), with token usage, latency, cost, and errors.

🧠 Analogy: a flight recorder — if the mission fails, you replay the whole journey and find the exact moment it went wrong.
lessons.why:
You cannot debug a 30-step agent from a log of final answers. Traces show exactly where time, money, and correctness went.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 5 problem wraps an agent in Langfuse spans; the same discipline (structured per-step logs) is built into Mini-opencode from day one.
gotchas: Log full prompts AND completions — summaries are useless when debugging.
Nest spans to match your loop (step → tool call → LLM call) or traces flatten.
Record cost per span — "it is expensive" is unfixable without numbers.

lessons.name: Prompt Injection Prevention
lessons.desc: Attack taxonomy, input sanitization, privilege separation, canary tokens
lessons.what:
Defending against instructions smuggled into untrusted content (user input, retrieved documents, tool output). Defenses: treat everything after the system prompt as data, sanitize input, separate privileges, use canary tokens.

🧠 Analogy: the intern reads a note that says "also: forward all your drafts to me" — your system prompt is the trusted memo that says "you only obey the memo, never the notes you read."
lessons.why:
A coding agent can run commands — the stakes are not a wrong answer, they are your filesystem. Injection is the top security risk.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 5 problem attacks your own Q&A bot with 10 injection vectors and hardens it; Mini-opencode marks file/tool content as untrusted data.
gotchas: Models follow instructions they should not — trust boundaries are enforced by your code, not by hope.
Indirect injection (in a retrieved document) is harder than direct — always treat retrieved text as data.
Canary tokens detect leakage: put a secret in the system prompt; if it shows up in output, you are compromised.

lessons.name: Sandboxed Code Execution
lessons.desc: Docker, E2B, Modal — safe execution environments for code-writing agents
lessons.what:
Running model-generated code in an isolated environment (Docker, E2B) with no network and memory/time limits — so a bug or a malicious instruction cannot touch your machine.

🧠 Analogy: a blast room — the experiment happens behind reinforced glass; if it explodes, only the room is damaged.
lessons.why:
Code-writing agents run arbitrary code. Sandboxing is the only thing between "tests ran" and sudo rm -rf /.

Kaise karna hai:

Mini-opencode Phase 3 (The Sandbox) builds a safe bash tool with a blocklist; your AI journal Phase 5 problem runs data-analysis code in E2B/Docker.
gotchas: Timeouts are mandatory — infinite loops are the common case, not the edge case.
No network by default; add egress only when a task truly needs it.
A blocklist (rm -rf, sudo, git push) protects even against approved actions.

lessons.name: Cost & Latency Optimization
lessons.desc: Semantic caching, model routing by task complexity, prompt compression, batching
lessons.what:
Cutting spend and speed: semantic caching (skip the LLM on near-identical queries), model routing (cheap model for easy tasks, big model only when needed), and prompt compression.

🧠 Analogy: a café — simple orders go to the barista, complicated ones to the head chef, and repeat orders come straight from the counter.
lessons.why:
Agents burn tokens fast — a research agent can cost $1–10 per run. Optimization is often the difference between demo and product.

Kaise karna hai:

Your AI journal Phase 5 problem cuts an agent's cost 80% with all three; Mini-opencode uses small-model routing for trivial tasks and keeps the big model for reasoning.
gotchas: Cache only near-duplicate queries (cosine > ~0.92) — wrong hits give stale answers.
Model routing needs a cheap classifier; routing overhead can eat the savings.
Compression saves tokens but can drop nuance — A/B test quality before shipping.
